title: A Smile for the Well
premise: Dominic Winterbourne returns to Hollowmere House to appraise it for sale, only to find her childhood imaginary friend, Wren, waiting on the porch—aged not a day in twenty years. The house's founders built a ritual into its walls that feeds on forgotten memories, and Dominic's decade of rationalizing the noises was itself a symptom of the house erasing her. As frost patterns spread across every mirror, she must reconstruct what she gave up: a twin sister the town agreed never existed. To end it, she must complete the founders' interrupted ritual—not to banish the house, but to name what it swallowed, choosing truth over the comfortable lie of being an only child, even if remembering costs her Wren forever.
about_author: Mirabel Vane is the pen name of a former architectural conservator who spent years cataloguing abandoned properties across northern England before turning to horror. She writes in unheated rooms, on the theory that a little cold keeps the sentences honest.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Dominic arrives at Hollowmere House for a routine survey, narrating in close third person. The house measures wrong—rooms larger inside than out—and her instruments return readings of her own heartbeat. Emotional beat: professional detachment beginning to crack as she recognizes the porch swing from dreams she's never admitted having.

chapters.title: Wren on the Porch
chapters.summary: A child sits on the porch swing, unchanged after twenty years, greeting Dominic by a nickname no one living knows. POV shifts between Dominic's terror and a strange, shameful relief. Emotional beat: the collision of adult skepticism with a longing she buried so deep she forgot burying it.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter: Dominic's decade of rationalizations—settling foundations, wind in chimneys, a neighbor's dog. Each explanation is recounted in her own past journal entries, which grow increasingly desperate. Emotional beat: the reader sees what Dominic can't—that the explanations were written in someone else's handwriting.

chapters.title: The Founders' Ledger
chapters.summary: In the cellar, Dominic finds the 1893 ledger of Aldous and Mercy Fenwick, the house's builders, describing a 'keeping ritual' to preserve what the town wished forgotten. The final page is torn out. Emotional beat: scholarly curiosity curdling into recognition—the ledger lists payments made by families, including one signed 'Winterbourne.'

chapters.title: What the Town Agreed
chapters.summary: Dominic visits the village archive and the last elderly resident, Mrs. Calloway, who goes white at the name Winterbourne. Everyone speaks of the family as if it had one child. Emotional beat: gaslighting made communal—Dominic begins doubting her own memory while sensing the whole town is complicit in the same forgetting.

chapters.title: Frost Patterns
chapters.summary: Overnight frost blooms on every mirror and window in patterns too deliberate for weather: they form letters, then a child's drawing of two girls holding hands. Wren appears indoors now, closer each time. Emotional beat: dread shifting from external threat to internal invasion—the house is writing on Dominic herself.

chapters.title: The Room That Isn't Measured
chapters.summary: Surveying upstairs, Dominic finds a door her floor plans don't show, behind wallpaper that matches her childhood bedroom exactly. Inside: two beds, two toothbrushes, dust undisturbed for decades. Emotional beat: grief arriving before understanding—her body reacts to the room as homecoming.

chapters.title: Wren's Bargain
chapters.summary: Wren finally explains: she isn't imaginary; she's what remains of the keeping ritual, a vessel holding everything the house took. She offers Dominic a choice—finish the appraisal, leave, forget again, and be safe. Emotional beat: temptation rendered tender; safety has never sounded so much like dying.

chapters.title: Mrs. Calloway's Confession
chapters.summary: Calloway, dying and frightened, admits the town paid the Fenwicks to 'keep' an inconvenient child—a Winterbourne twin born wrong, embarrassing, erased. She gives Dominic the torn ledger page. Emotional beat: horror relocating from the supernatural to the human; the monster kept receipts.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: The recovered page describes the ritual's completion: the kept thing must be named aloud by blood within the house before the first hard frost sets—or the house keeps the rememberer too. The frost is three days out. Emotional beat: resolve forming alongside terror; knowledge is now a deadline.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: The house fights back: roads out of the village loop back to Hollowmere, her phone shows calls she never made apologizing to clients, her car's registration reads a name that isn't hers. Emotional beat: identity erosion—Dominic realizes the house has been editing her for years, and is accelerating.

chapters.title: The Second Bed
chapters.summary: Sleeping in the hidden room, Dominic dreams in first person as the erased twin—running through these halls, laughing with Wren, being carried down to the cellar by gentle hands. She wakes with mud on her feet. Emotional beat: the wall between herself and the sister dissolving; memory returning as possession.

chapters.title: Aldous Fenwick's Notes
chapters.summary: Reading deeper into the ledger, Dominic learns the founders didn't invent the ritual—they inherited it, and Mercy left annotations condemning it, describing how to unmake rather than keep. Her notes are annotated in turn by later hands, angrier ones. Emotional beat: hope with a body count; every previous attempt to undo it failed fatally.

chapters.title: The Neighbors' Lights
chapters.summary: Villagers begin appearing at the house's fence line at night, standing silently, watching windows. They don't cross the property line but they don't leave. Emotional beat: siege atmosphere—the community's forgetting requires her silence, and they've come to ensure it.

chapters.title: Wren Unravels
chapters.summary: As Dominic remembers more, Wren begins to fray—flickering, speaking in the twin's voice mid-sentence, forgetting which of them she is. She confesses she was never a friend; she's the container, and naming the twin will empty her. Emotional beat: loyalty vs. truth made flesh—saving her sister means killing the only friend who waited.

chapters.title: The Cellar Keepsake
chapters.summary: Following Mercy's annotations, Dominic opens the cellar's false wall and finds the kept things: shoes, drawings, a lock of hair, and small clay figures for every family who paid—including one still warm. Emotional beat: revulsion and pity entwined; the house is a reliquary of everyone's convenient amnesia.

chapters.title: First Frost Eve
chapters.summary: The night before the hard frost, the villagers finally enter, led by Calloway's son, insisting gently that there was never a second child, that she should rest, that they'll take her home. The house hums approval. Emotional beat: the climax's threshold—Dominic must refuse kindness weaponized, alone, in the dark.

chapters.title: The Ritual Interrupted
chapters.summary: In the cellar, Dominic begins Mercy's unmaking rite as the frost writes itself up the walls and the villagers fill the stairwell, murmuring her old explanations back at her in her own voice. Wren holds the door, unraveling badly. Emotional beat: climax—every rationalization she ever told herself deployed against her at once.

chapters.title: Her Name Was Iris
chapters.summary: At the rite's crux, Dominic must speak the kept name aloud. She does—Iris Winterbourne—and the house convulses; mirrors shatter outward; the villagers collapse weeping into remembered grief. Wren empties into light, whispering thank you. Emotional beat: catharsis purchased at the cost of the friend who waited twenty years.

chapters.title: Aftermath of the Thaw
chapters.summary: Dawn. The house measures true for the first time; the hidden room is just a room; the frost melts into ordinary water. The villagers disperse, hollowed but free, some furious. Dominic stands in the doorway of the second bedroom holding a child's drawing of two girls. Emotional beat: raw, exhausted clarity—truth won, and it hurts like truth does.

chapters.title: Appraisal Complete
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Dominic files her survey with an addendum documenting the hidden room and the Fenwick ledger, ending her career's habit of explaining away. She signs both her names for the first time. Emotional beat: quiet reclamation—identity rebuilt on remembered ground rather than comfortable fog.

chapters.title: A Smile for the Well
chapters.summary: Final chapter: demolishing the well behind the house, workers find nothing—but that night, on the porch of Dominic's new flat, a child's voice says her old nickname once, kindly, and is gone. She smiles, grieves, and leaves the light on anyway. Emotional beat: bittersweet coda—some loyalties outlast their vessels, and love doesn't require believing the lie.
